extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and news professionals studying how news is produced
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how news organizations and routines select, shape, and disseminate events as news — i.e., the organizational, professional, and spatial criteria that constitute 'newsworthiness'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness criteria (immediacy, importance, significance, interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: News items might be measured against statistical indices of importance, significance, and interest and immediacy (e.g., an editor could assign numerical values and compute a regression-based 'newsworthiness' score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents this as a hypothetical/objective schema (assign numerical values to importance, significance, and interest and use a regression equation). It is offered as one conceivable method for deciding what is news and contrasts with the social/organizational processes the author emphasizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement at central institutional sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Place reporters at central, legitimated locations (police headquarters, federal courthouse, City Hall, Board of Estimate calendars, etc.) because these sites routinely yield occurrences deemed newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Systematic location at central sites makes it efficient to find events; these placements both facilitate reporting and reaffirm public legitimacy of those institutions. Example: assigning a salaried City Hall reporter increases likelihood of stories from City Hall being selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization via wire services and Day Books
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of wire services (Associated Press, UPI) and their instruments (Day Books) as primary connectives between newsrooms and wider world events; Day Books list anticipated events so media can decide coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: Wire services provide feeds and story leads; practices like 'rip-and-read' (reading wire copy verbatim) and getting events listed in Day Books are professionally significant. Anti-pattern: overreliance ('rip-and-read') reduces independent reporting and narrows the news net.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic imperative to fill the news product
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations must provide stories to fill pre-specified space/time (newspaper columns, Sunday editions, television airtime) because the product is organized around advertising schedules and contractual obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: editors will find or manufacture material to satisfy these constraints; slow news periods lead to discarding some information or seeking more entertainment-oriented stories. Historical examples: Sunday edition ad demands, TV programming obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: News net selectivity (mesh holes favor big events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'news net' metaphor: the net has holes and its mesh design determines what is captured — current systems are designed to catch 'big fish' (major events) and often miss small-scale occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: A narrower, more expensive mesh would catch smaller events, but current investment choices privilege large, legitimated occurrences. This explains systematic omissions (e.g., student plagiarism vs university administrative decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial preference for staff-produced material over stringers/wire items
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and photo editors prefer copy, photographs, and footage produced by their staff rather than by stringers or wire services, even when outside material may be superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: photography editors choosing staff shots over wire-service photos; TV stations favoring their crew footage and chastising crews when network footage is better. Practice: stringers are used mainly in dire need (e.g., unexpected night disturbances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic territoriality and beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the world into territorial responsibilities (beats, bureaus) so reporters cover specific geographic areas and institutions; territorial divisions reflect the organization's notion of its 'news mission' and assumed reader interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Geographic territoriality is central; it organizes reporter dispersion, determines what occurrences are accessible, and influences selection. Examples: suburban stringers/bureaus to capture suburban readers; Washington or state bureaus for distant coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement of legitimated institutions through reporting practices
rubrics_metrics.description: News practices (placement of reporters, reliance on centralized files, wire-service patterns) make occurrences at legitimated institutions more likely to be defined as news, thereby reaffirming those institutions' public legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: Organizations that host beats are privileged; occurrences in unassigned locations or among marginalized groups are less likely to be covered. This functions ideologically to legitimate status quo groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal newsroom competition and negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactions within the newsroom bureaucracy — reporters competing for assignments and editors negotiating to get copy placed — shape what is identified as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Editors and bureau chiefs 'wheel and deal' to get by-lines into the paper; competition among editors for assignments influences selection and placement. The bureaucracy of assignments and deadlines is a determining factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and routine practices (deadlines, rhythms) to winnow information
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations objectify deadlines and create rhythms of work and classifications of newsworthy occurrences, which reduce idiosyncrasy in what becomes news and provide routine ways to select and weed information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Using past experiences, organizations classify occurrence-types and use deadlines/rhythms to manage glut of information. These routines shape the 'news of the day' and the negotiation of overlapping responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source selection and the construction of a 'web of facticity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Reportorial methods create a 'web of facticity' — mutual constitution of news sources and facts — by identifying certain people/institutions as appropriate sources and generating quasi-legitimated leaders when legitimated leaders are unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Methods include corroboration chains and preferential sourcing; this serves to maintain credibility but can legitimize particular perspectives and marginalize others. Chapter 5 (referenced) examines how this legitimates the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational style and framing in broadcast and film
rubrics_metrics.description: Television uses specific representational styles (shots, narrative structures) and professional practices to present reporters as impartial arbiters; styles differ by event type (natural disasters, riots, demonstrations, legitimated leaders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: How film is handled meets organizational needs and contributes to a particular framing of events; choices of shots/narratives affect interpretation and perceived neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication and mutual reinforcement across media and wire services
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations and wire services frequently duplicate and complement one another's efforts and 'borrow' stories, which increases the probability of similar coverage across outlets rather than independent, diverse reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: night editors checking competitors' first editions to learn missed stories and ordering rewrites; local outlets using wire-service accounts as primary leads. This fosters professional consensus about what is news and shared 'holes' in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed reader interests: localities, organizations, topics, and persons/roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Three assumptions guide reporter dispersion: (1) readers are interested in occurrences at specific localities, (2) they care about activities of specific organizations, and (3) they are interested in specific topics and persons (e.g., movie stars, presidents, television personalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: These assumptions inform beat structure, story selection, and the kinds of occurrences pursued. They are organizationally embedded expectations shaping news mission and coverage priorities.
